X.notes: Strengths: src/text.mjs is a minimal, correct implementation. It passed every probe I ran: the spec examples, 'ﬁle Ⅻ'->'file-xii' (NFKD), 'İstanbul', CJK input -> '', '   abc',3 -> '…', 2**53, 3.0, and BigInt/Infinity/NaN/'5' for max (all give RangeError). Validation order (TypeError before RangeError) is sensible. npm test passes 4/4 in a temp copy. Defects: src/text.mjs:6 writes the combining-mark range as raw literal U+0300/U+036F characters (bytes CC 80 / CD AF). These render invisibly as `[̀-ͯ]` and are hard to read or edit safely, where ̀-ͯ would be clear. The type check is duplicated at lines 2 and 12, and the error messages don't say which function threw. The tests (test/text.test.mjs) cover all spec examples, exact length (11), max=1, an empty string, and a good list of invalid max values (0, -1, 1.5, NaN, '5', undefined). But they are grouped into 4 coarse tests, test truncate's TypeError with only one value, have no digit-preservation case, and have no case that tells NFKD apart from NFD. Y.notes: Strengths: src/text.mjs has the clearest code of the three. It names its regex constants with \u escapes (lines 1-4), puts the type check in a shared assertString helper (lines 6-10), and its error messages say what was received. The tests (8, all pass) include 'ﬁle Ⅻ'->'file-xii' (test/text.test.mjs:10), the only case in any solution that checks NFKD rather than NFD. They also cover digits, exact length, max=1, Infinity and null for max, and both functions' TypeErrors. Defect: src/text.mjs:25 builds the RangeError message with `${String(max)}`. For a max that cannot be converted to a primitive, that call throws first, so the function no longer throws the RangeError the spec requires. I confirmed this: truncate('abc', Object.create(null)) throws 'TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value', and an object whose toString throws leaks that Error instead of a RangeError. The case is rare, but the spec violation comes from the extra diagnostic code. All other probes match X and Z. README.md is a one-line placeholder with no usage.

Z is last. It is equally correct and has clean, compact source, but its tests are two monolithic blocks with thinner negative-case coverage, its type check is duplicated, and its error messages are generic.

All three share the same placeholder README, so docs don't separate them.

Running NFKD before lowercasing gives better slugs for compatibility characters (ℌ, ℂ, 𝐀), which Y and Z silently drop. X also has the most thorough and best-structured tests, including a dedicated NFKD test, and the cleanest named-constant code. Its one robustness flaw is String(max) in the error message, which can turn the required RangeError into a TypeError for null-prototype objects; that is contrived. Z and Y tie on overall score. Z ranks above Y because its code is cleaner: the combining-mark range is escaped, whereas Y embeds invisible raw combining characters in the regex at src/text.mjs:14, a real readability and maintainability defect. Z's explicit test path is also more portable than the glob script. Y's test suite is somewhat broader and better grouped than Z's two monolithic tests, but the extra cases only add to the same spec coverage and do not offset the code-quality issue. None of the three has a meaningful README.

X.notes: Strengths: meets the spec on every core path I probed. add joins and trims; ids come from a persisted lastId, so they are never reused (also after clear-done empties the list). list sorts by id. done is idempotent. For done/remove, -1 and 0 are integers and give 'Error: not found #-1/#0' with exit 1, the strict reading of the spec. Corrupt JSON exits 3 and the file is never written. Usage goes to stderr with exit 2 and Object.hasOwn guards against inherited names. Atomic write uses a hidden temp file in the same folder, and the temp file is removed on failure (todo.mjs:46-55). Cleanest design of the three: commands are pure (data,args)->{data,out} functions and main owns load/save in one place (todo.mjs:68-113), with no IO duplication. Tests: 25 cases, all passing. They strip TODO_FILE from the inherited env, use an ok() helper that fails loudly when a setup step fails, and cover 0/-1, leading zeros, 1e2, LIST, four corrupt variants across all five commands with a byte-exact untouched check, the default cwd file, file creation on first write, and no leftover temp files. README is the most complete: per-command errors, id parsing rules, the data shape, the literal usage text and an exit-code table. Defects: load runs before argument validation (todo.mjs:104), so 'add ""' or 'done abc' on a corrupt file gives exit 3 instead of 2. The spec allows this reading. isValidStore (todo.mjs:23-26) does not validate the todo elements: {"lastId":0,"todos":[null]} makes list crash with a TypeError stack trace (todo.mjs:77), and add happily writes into that file. lastId is not reconciled with the existing ids, so a hand-edited file with a low lastId produces duplicate ids. I/O errors such as EISDIR are rethrown as raw stack traces (todo.mjs:109). clear-done on a missing file creates the file, which is harmless.

Y.notes: Strengths: fully spec-compliant in my probes, including -1 and 0 giving 'not found' with exit 1. Argument validation runs before the data read, so 'add ""' on a corrupt file still exits 2. Most robust loader (todo.mjs:38-42): it requires an integer nextId, an array of todos, and each todo to have an integer id below nextId, a string text and a boolean done. Malformed or hand-edited files therefore become 'corrupt data file' (exit 3, untouched) instead of crashing. Unexpected I/O errors are turned into 'Error: <msg>' with exit 1 rather than a stack trace (todo.mjs:121-122), and the README documents this. The temp file sits in the same folder and is removed on failure (todo.mjs:46-55). Code is compact and readable. Defects: the test suite is the thinnest, with 12 tests. It has no out-of-order list sort test, does not cover 0/-1 or leading zeros, and only lightly checks default-file behaviour. Its beforeEach creates a temp dir per test and never removes it (test/todo.test.mjs:22-25), which leaks directories. done always rewrites the file, even when the todo is already done, and clear-done always writes and so creates the file when it is missing (todo.mjs:89-90, 103). Both are harmless. The README is accurate but brief: it does not spell out the invalid id and not found messages, and it describes exit 3 as only 'not valid JSON' although bad shape also triggers it.

Z.notes: Strengths: all core commands match the spec. Argument validation comes before the data read. The persisted nextId is reconciled as max(nextId, maxId+1), which guards against hand-edited files (todo.mjs:41-42). It avoids needless writes: an already-done todo or 'Cleared 0' does not touch or create the file. The temp file is a hidden dotfile in the same folder. Object.hasOwn handles 'toString'. Tests: 30 well-organised describe/test cases using exact {code,stdout,stderr} deepEqual. They cover out-of-order list sort, corrupt input for every command, bad-shape JSON, arg-before-data precedence, the default cwd file, TODO_FILE and no leftover temp files. README is clear, with per-command examples and an exit-code table that lists the messages. Defects: parseId uses /^\d+$/ (todo.mjs:53), so '-1', an integer that does not exist, gives 'Error: invalid id' with exit 2 instead of 'Error: not found #-1' with exit 1. The test suite enshrines this deviation from the spec (test/todo.test.mjs:39). It also accepts '0' as not found, which is inconsistent. A todos array containing null crashes the max-id reduce with a raw TypeError stack trace (todo.mjs:41). I/O errors such as EISDIR also surface as stack traces (todo.mjs:116). save does not remove the temp file if the write or rename fails (todo.mjs:46-50).

reasoning:
All three pass their own suites on Node 26 (X 25/25, Y 12/12, Z 30/30) and implement the same core design: a persisted id counter, an atomic temp-file-plus-rename write in the same folder, and Object.hasOwn command dispatch.

X ranks first. It follows the spec on every path I probed, including treating -1 and 0 as integers that are not found. It has the cleanest architecture: pure command functions, with load and save done once in main. Its tests are the strongest, with explicit edge cases, byte-exact checks that corrupt files stay untouched across four corrupt variants, and env isolation. Its README is the most complete. Its weaknesses are mostly outside the spec: no element-level shape validation, so a hand-edited [null] crashes; no reconciliation of lastId with existing ids; raw stack traces on I/O errors; and corrupt-file errors taking precedence over invalid-argument errors, which the spec permits.

Y ranks second. It is the most correct and the most robust: strict validation of each todo, graceful handling of unexpected I/O errors, argument validation before the data read, and -1 handled per the spec. Its test suite is noticeably thinner and leaks temp directories, and its README is terse.

Z ranks third. Its code and README are good and its tests are broad. However, it rejects '-1' as 'invalid id' with exit 2, where the spec, read literally, requires 'not found #-1' with exit 1, and its tests lock that behaviour in. Its robustness is also the weakest: a stack trace on a null element, stack traces on I/O errors, and no temp-file cleanup on failure.

X.notes:

Writes go to a temp file in the same folder and are renamed over the data file. Invalid JSON and a wrong shape both give exit 3, and every command leaves the file byte-identical. Usage starts with 'Usage:', and Object.hasOwn rejects prototype names such as toString and __proto__. '-1' and '0' count as integers and give 'not found', which matches the strict reading of the spec.

Strengths:
- Cleanest design of the three (todo.mjs:68-95): each command is a pure function returning {data,out}, and main (97-113) does the only load and save.
- save cleans up the temp file on failure (46-55).
- Best test suite. An ok() helper asserts that every setup step succeeds (test:21-25), and every result is checked exactly with deepEqual on {code,stdout,stderr}.
- Corrupt-file tests cover 4 contents x all 5 commands with a byte-level check that the file is untouched (186-203).
- Also tested: sort when the file stores todos out of order (84-89), id reuse after clear-done (119-125), 0/-1 and leading zeros, the default todo.json in cwd with TODO_FILE stripped from env, and that no temp files are left behind. Temp dirs are cleaned with t.after.
- README is thorough and accurate: per-command examples, id parsing rules, data file shape, exit-code table.

Defects:
- Errors that are not CliError are rethrown (todo.mjs:109). If TODO_FILE is a directory or its parent folder is missing, the user gets a raw Node stack trace with exit 1.
- isValidStore (23-26) checks only the top-level shape. A hand-edited {"lastId":1,"todos":[null]} crashes list with a TypeError. A lastId lower than an existing id leads to duplicate ids.
- clear-done always writes, so on a missing file it creates the file even when nothing was cleared (91-94).
- load runs before the arguments are checked (104), so 'add ""' on a corrupt file returns 3, not 2. The spec allows either order.

- Catch-all handler (116-123) turns I/O errors such as EISDIR or a missing folder into a clean 'Error: ...' line with exit 1, not a stack trace. The README documents this.

- Arguments are checked before the file is read.

Defects:

- Every command does its own load and save, so the pattern is repeated.
- clear-done always writes, creating the file even when nothing was cleared (100-105).
- Weakest test suite:
  - Only 12 tests.
  - beforeEach calls mkdtemp but nothing ever removes the dirs (test:22-25), so each run leaves temp folders behind.
  - Setup run() calls are never checked.
  - add with whitespace only checks the exit code (34).
  - No test for sort order when the file stores todos out of order (append order makes the current check trivial).
  - No test of id reuse after clear-done.
  - The test named 'writes atomically' (109) only checks for leftover files and also covers the default path.
- README is accurate but brief: one-line examples and a table, no TODO_FILE example, and it does not explain how ids are parsed.

Z.notes:
Tests: 30/30 pass (run in a temp copy). Spec: the core commands, outputs, exit codes, atomic temp-file-and-rename writes, usage text and corrupt-JSON handling are correct.

Strengths:
- Skips writes that change nothing: done on an already-done todo (todo.mjs:84-87) and clear-done with 0 cleared (101). clear-done on a missing file does not create it.
- nextId is reconciled with the highest stored id (41-42), which protects against duplicate ids in hand-edited files.
- Well-organised tests: describe blocks, t.after cleanup, exact {code,stdout,stderr} checks, corrupt JSON across all commands with the file left untouched, an argument-before-file-read test (249-256), toString as a command name, TODO_FILE vs the default path, and no temp files left behind.
- Clear README with an exit-code and message table.

Defects:
- parseId uses /^\d+$/ (53), so 'done -1' prints 'Error: invalid id' with exit 2. The spec reserves 'invalid id' for missing or non-integer ids; any integer that does not exist should be 'not found #-1' with exit 1. The tests lock this deviation in (test:39).

- The random-code loop has no attempt cap (negligible risk).
- Test gaps: no non-object JSON body test, no non-ASCII redirect test, and the rate-limit test mixes only 415 and 201.

Z.notes:
Tests: 83/83 pass across 6 files. It passed every process-level probe: listening line, default ./data.db, 415 (missing, text/plain, application/jsonx), mixed-case and charset content types accepted, 413 at 10241 bytes but not 10240, chunked 413 sent before the body ends, 400 for invalid, empty, array, null or string bodies, 2048/2049, the code pattern including null, number, empty and unicode, 409, the 21st POST giving 429 with 400/413/415 counted, X-Forwarded-For ignored, stats types, 404s, DELETE ordering (401 before 404), unset or empty ADMIN_TOKEN, 204 with no body, 302 plus clicks, all traversal variants returning 404, a malformed path giving 400, and persistence.

Strengths:
- Cohesive lib/ split: routing in server.mjs:17-38; http helpers with an early 413 plus Connection: close in lib/http.mjs:40-61; validation and handlers in lib/links.mjs; a bounded rate limiter with a sweep in lib/rate-limit.mjs:7-25; safe static serving in lib/static.mjs:20-31.
- Control characters are rejected up front (lib/links.mjs:10,14). Non-ASCII targets get a percent-encoded Location while ASCII URLs are sent exactly as stored (lib/links.mjs:87). This was verified.
- Token comparison uses timingSafeEqual over SHA-256 digests, so no length leak (lib/links.mjs:68-73).
- PORT is validated with exit code 1 (server.mjs:88-92). createServer is injectable (port 0, :memory:). Every response carries nosniff, and redirects send Cache-Control: no-store.
- Tests cover child-process startup and persistence, chunked 413 over a raw socket, traversal over raw paths, the limiter under a 5000-hit flood, frontend fetch logic with fakes plus an end-to-end run against the real server, and a static scan for HTML sinks.
- The frontend is polished and accessible: aria-live, a copy button, safe hrefs, and textContent only. Verified in a browser.
- The README is thorough and accurate: config table, check order, rate-limit semantics, routing caveats, project layout.

Defects (minor):
- test/backend-smoke.test.mjs largely duplicates api.test.mjs, and line 66 has a weak `[200,404].includes(root.status)` assertion.
- app.js DOM rendering has no unit test beyond the static sink grep.
- index.html:7-9 loads Google Fonts, an external request for an otherwise self-contained app.
- The limiter keeps blocked stamps (the last 21), so a client that keeps retrying stays blocked. This is stricter than the spec and the README does not spell it out.
- A URL with leading whitespace is accepted and echoed verbatim into Location.
- HEAD returns 405.

X.notes: Its own suite passes 27/27. My black-box probe found 5 deviations. Strengths: the rate limit is checked before the 415 check, so every POST counts, rejected ones included (server.mjs:220). The token check uses timingSafeEqual (server.mjs:180-185). There is a traversal guard with a decode, NUL and prefix check (server.mjs:187-203). The 413 is enforced on both Content-Length and the streamed size, then the connection is closed (server.mjs:95-118, 284). The SQLite unique-violation path is handled atomically. Defects: (1) The redirect always normalises the URL with `new URL(row.url).href` (server.mjs:255), so a stored `https://example.com` redirects to `https://example.com/`, and host case, dot segments and default ports also get rewritten. The spec says the Location is the stored url. (2) isHttpUrl (server.mjs:140-148) only parses with WHATWG URL, so it accepts non-absolute or ill-formed inputs such as `http:x.com`, `http:/x.com` and ` https://e.com` (leading space); all return 201. (3) HEAD /<code> is routed like GET and increments clicks (server.mjs:248). (4) An invalid PORT silently falls back to 3000 (server.mjs:300). (5) It uses sync fs.statSync and readFileSync in the request path, and every redirect stats public/ first. (6) README says `npm test # runs: node --test`, but the script is `node --test test/*.test.mjs`. Any non-GET request to an unknown path returns 405, which is broader than the README claims. Tests are strong: a fake DOM whose innerHTML setter throws (frontend.test.mjs), traversal variants, a 21st and 22nd request returning 429 after mixed rejected requests, and a spawn test covering PORT, DB_FILE and ADMIN_TOKEN. Gaps: no window-recovery test (no clock injection), no exact 10240-byte boundary test, and the form wiring is not tested. Everything sits in one 309-line file. It is readable but monolithic.

Y.notes: Its own suite passes 34/34. My black-box probe found only one deviation. Defect: the redirect always sends `new URL(url).href` (server.mjs:70), so `https://example.com` becomes `https://example.com/` and other URLs get canonicalised. The spec wants the stored url, and normalising only non-header-safe URLs would have been enough. Minor: code-pattern paths are routed before static files (server.mjs:87-89), so an extensionless file in public/ would be shadowed. The duplicate check depends on SQLite extended errcodes 1555 and 2067 (store.mjs:279); it works but is brittle. `DB_FILE ?? './data.db'` lets an empty string through. Strengths: clean modular layout (src/store, rate-limit, static, http-utils) with small focused functions. URL validation is strict: it requires an http(s):// prefix, rejects whitespace and control characters, and calls URL.canParse (server.mjs:15-27). The token is compared as a SHA-256 hash with timingSafeEqual. Responses carry nosniff. PORT is validated, and tables are created on start. The rate limiter takes an injectable clock and prunes idle keys (rate-limit.mjs). Tests are thorough on the API: exact 10240-byte boundary, streamed 413 without Content-Length plus Connection: close, rolling-window recovery, 429 before 415, flood behaviour, non-ASCII redirect, traversal against a fixture public dir, 405 and 404 JSON, and a spawn test. Frontend fetch logic in api.js is well tested, including network failure, a non-JSON error body, and a 2xx with an unreadable body. The rendering code in app.js has no unit tests, only a source grep for innerHTML. The README is excellent: a check-order table, a config table, frontend notes and the file layout. In the browser, the UI worked end to end and inserted all text safely.

Z.notes: Its own suite passes 54/54, and it passed every check in my black-box probe. Strengths: the redirect keeps the stored URL as is and percent-encodes only values that are not header-safe (src/app.mjs:39, 114), so Location matches the stored url. URL validation is strict: prefix regex, no whitespace or control characters, a non-empty hostname, and a length cap (app.mjs:41-50). Codes are inserted with `INSERT OR IGNORE` plus a changes check (store.mjs:317-333), which is atomic and avoids relying on errcodes. Request bodies are drained on 415 and 413 so error responses arrive cleanly (http.mjs:187-224). The rate limit is checked first, so every POST counts. The token is compared as a SHA-256 hash with timingSafeEqual. HTML is served with nosniff and a CSP header. The entry point validates PORT and shuts down cleanly on SIGINT and SIGTERM (server.mjs). The layout is modular: entry, app, http and store. Tests are the most complete of the three. They are table-driven for bad URLs and codes, include a chunked 413, use clock injection to show that rejected POSTs count and the window recovers, confirm GET is not rate-limited, cover DELETE with and without a token, and include traversal, non-ASCII redirect, and a spawn test that checks persistence across restart through DB_FILE. Frontend tests cover fetch, rendering with a fake DOM whose innerHTML throws, and the init() form wiring. Minor issues: createApp has no default for its options object (app.mjs:79). server.test.mjs picks a random port in 30000-50000, which could collide. There is no exact 10240-byte boundary test. The frontend has no busy or disabled state and shows createdAt as a raw ISO string. GET /api/links returns 404 rather than 405. The README is concise and accurate, with an env table, an API table, notes on X-Forwarded-For, a coverage script and the file layout, but it is less detailed than Y's. In the browser, the UI worked end to end; native pattern validation blocks bad codes before submit.

reasoning: All three suites pass and all three cover the core spec. I ranked them on my black-box probe results (spec edge cases), strictness and test depth. Z ranks first. It was the only one with zero probe failures. Its redirect keeps the stored URL, encoding only when needed. Its validation and storage are the most careful (INSERT OR IGNORE, body draining, CSP, graceful shutdown). It has the widest tests, including frontend init() wiring and persistence across a real restart. Y ranks second and is very close on engineering quality. It has the best README and clean modules, and its API tests are excellent (clock injection, exact 10240 boundary, streamed 413). But it always canonicalises the redirect Location, so `https://example.com` becomes `https://example.com/`, which breaks 'Location set to the stored url'. Its rendering code is also not unit-tested. X ranks third. It is solid and secure in most ways and has good tests. But it has the most spec deviations: the same Location normalisation, looser URL validation (accepts `http:x.com`, `http:/x.com` and a leading-space URL), and HEAD requests counting as clicks. It also lacks a window-recovery test, a minor README command claim is wrong, and everything is in one file.
